1. Reservation-to-invoice rate: of the reservations of the last {0} days whose outcome is already known (invoiced, expired or with the vehicle sold to someone else), {1} ended in an invoice.
2. Quotation-to-reservation rate: a quotation is valid only on the day it is made. {0} of the quotations ended that same day in a reservation by the same person for the same vehicle.
3. Active reservations: each one adds its probability of being invoiced. If a vehicle has several reservations, the probability of selling it is 1 − (1 − p)^n, because it is sold only once.

4. New flow: in the last {0} days, for each {3}-day period, {1} quotations and {2} reservations without a quotation came in. {1} × {4} + {2} = {5} new reservations are expected, invoiced with the rate of point 1 at an average ticket of {6}.
5. 90% range: each reservation is a yes or no with its probability (variance p·(1 − p)) and the new flow is treated as a Poisson process (variance equal to the mean).

1. Completion rate by stage: of the purchases of the last {0} days whose outcome is already known (finished or lost), the share of those that reached each stage and ended in the inventory is counted. From creation, {1}.

2. Stages: the purchase does not keep a status history, so each stage is dated with the record that produced it (inspection, first appraisal, contract signature, last document, payment receipt, transfer documents and closing). That tells which stage each purchase was in on any date.

3. Open purchases: each one adds P(finish | stage) × P(close within the next {0} days). The second one comes from the finished purchases that took, from that stage, longer than this one already has: the share that closed within the horizon.

4. New flow: in the last {0} days, {1} purchases were started per {2}-day period. {3} are finished and, since a purchase that starts on any day of the horizon has to go through every stage before it ends, only {4} make it in time: {5} vehicles, at an average price of {6}.
5. Amounts: each purchase is valued at its agreed price or, if it has none yet, at its last appraisal. The cash to pay subtracts what has already been paid to each person.
6. 90% range: each open purchase is a yes or no with its probability (variance p·(1 − p)) and the new flow is treated as a Poisson process (variance equal to the mean).
